title: Code World Model: Building World Models for Computation – Jacob Kahn, FAIR Meta
talk_summary: Meta FAIR trained a 32B dense model (CWM) to predict program execution traces as a chain-of-thought, so it can simulate code execution internally rather than only seeing syntax. They also describe a highly asynchronous RL post-training loop with queued models and trajectories, including swapping model checkpoints mid-trajectory to remove bottlenecks.

takeaways.technique: Execution-trace reasoning as a review/debug signal
takeaways.what_they_do: Model is trained to emit line-by-line execution traces (locals, frame separators) so it can predict program state transitions without running the code.

takeaways.technique: Asynchronous producer/consumer with queues instead of barriers
takeaways.what_they_do: Samplers produce trajectories and trainers consume them via queues; checkpoints and trajectories are queued eagerly so nothing waits for a full round to finish.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have cues. So we actually will have many models queued up to be input into a sampling system

takeaways.what_they_do: They replace the sampling model with a newer checkpoint while a trajectory is still interacting with the environment, accepting slight off-policy drift for throughput.
takeaways.evidence_quote: mid- trajectory I could totally swap out the model with the new checkpoint

takeaways.technique: Rejection sampling of failed agent traces for retraining/prompting
takeaways.what_they_do: They collect failed agentic reasoning traces on code tasks and feed them back into the model as SFT data.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can take a bunch of agentic reasoning traces on code tasks that failed and we can basically feed those back into the model

takeaways.what_they_do: CWM is deliberately given fewer tools and must learn to use the terminal well, matching a real engineer's environment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: CWM is a very bashoriented model. It has fewer tools than do other models
